title: Best Electrolyte Drink for a Hangover: 7 Brands Compared
excerpt: Pedialyte, Liquid IV, DripDrop, LMNT, Electrolit, Nuun, and Dioralyte compared for a hangover: what's in each, honest pros and cons, which to pick for how you feel, and when to see a doctor instead.
metaDescription: Pedialyte, Liquid IV, DripDrop, LMNT, Electrolit, Nuun and Dioralyte compared for hangovers: sodium, sugar, pros, cons, and which to pick.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** for a typical hangover, the best electrolyte drink is the one built like a medical oral rehydration solution: a moderate amount of sodium, some potassium, and a small amount of sugar to help your gut absorb it. Pedialyte, DripDrop, Electrolit, and Dioralyte all fit that description. Liquid IV is close to it with a bit more sugar. LMNT is very high in sodium with no sugar, which suits some people and not others. Nuun tablets are the lightest option and are fine for mild mornings. None of them cure a hangover. They help with one piece of it, the dehydration, and that piece is often smaller than the marketing suggests.

**The quick picks:**

- **Best all-round for a rough morning:** Pedialyte (or a store-brand oral rehydration solution with the same formula).
- **Best if you're also nauseous and struggling to keep fluids down:** DripDrop or Pedialyte, sipped slowly.
- **Best for taste and convenience:** Liquid IV.
- **Best if you avoid sugar or sweat heavily:** LMNT, though the sodium load is high.
- **Best for travel and mild hangovers:** Nuun tablets.
- **If you're in the UK or Europe:** Dioralyte from any pharmacy does the same job as Pedialyte.

> **When to see a doctor instead of reaching for a sports drink.** A hangover should improve through the day. Get medical help if you can't keep any fluids down for several hours, you're vomiting repeatedly or there's blood in your vomit, you've barely urinated in 8 hours or more, you feel faint or confused, your heart is racing and won't settle, or the symptoms are getting worse instead of better by the afternoon. If someone was very drunk the night before and is now hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin, that may be alcohol poisoning rather than a hangover. Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away. An electrolyte drink cannot fix any of those situations.

## Why Electrolytes Come Up at All After Drinking

Alcohol makes you pee more than you drink. It does this by suppressing **vasopressin** (also called antidiuretic hormone), the hormone that normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. With less of that signal, your kidneys let more water through, and you lose fluid along with some sodium and potassium. Add sweating in a hot bar, a few hours without water, and possibly vomiting or diarrhea, and you can wake up genuinely low on fluid.

That's the part an electrolyte drink can help with. Plain water rehydrates too, but water with the right balance of sodium and a little sugar is absorbed and retained more efficiently. That's the principle behind oral rehydration solution (ORS), which the World Health Organization developed to treat dehydration from diarrheal illness. Sodium and glucose are carried across the gut wall together, and water follows them. That mechanism is well established and is why drinks like Pedialyte exist.

### The part most "best hangover drink" lists skip

Dehydration is real after drinking, but it is not the main cause of a hangover. Researchers who have measured blood electrolytes and hormone levels in hungover people have generally not found a strong link between those numbers and how bad people feel. The bigger drivers appear to be the immune system's inflammatory response to alcohol, disrupted sleep, the effects of acetaldehyde (the toxic first breakdown product of alcohol), and congeners (by-products in darker drinks like bourbon and red wine).

So an electrolyte drink can make you feel better if you're actually dehydrated: dry mouth, dark urine, light-headed when you stand, headache that eases when you drink fluids. It won't do much for the foggy, inflamed, slept-badly feeling. Setting expectations there saves money and disappointment.

## The Main Electrolyte Drinks Compared

Here are the drinks people actually reach for, side by side. Figures are approximate per serving and come from the manufacturers' labels. Formulas change and flavors vary, so check the label on the product you buy.

| Drink | Serving | Sodium | Potassium | Sugar | Style |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pedialyte Classic | 12 fl oz | ~370 mg | ~280 mg | ~9 g | Medical-style ORS, ready to drink or powder |
| Liquid IV Hydration Multiplier | 1 stick in 16 fl oz | ~500 mg | ~370 mg | ~11 g | ORS-style powder, sweeter |
| DripDrop ORS | 1 stick in 8 fl oz | ~330 mg | ~185 mg | ~7 g | Medical-style ORS powder |
| LMNT | 1 stick in 16 to 32 fl oz | ~1,000 mg | ~200 mg | 0 g | High-sodium, sugar-free, adds magnesium |
| Electrolit | 1 bottle (~21 fl oz) | Moderate, ORS-range | Yes | Some glucose | Ready-to-drink ORS from Mexico |
| Nuun Sport | 1 tablet in 16 fl oz | ~300 mg | ~150 mg | ~1 g | Fizzy tablet, light electrolytes |
| Dioralyte (UK) | 1 sachet in 200 ml | ~60 mmol/L | ~20 mmol/L | Small amount of glucose | Pharmacy ORS sachet |
| Regular Gatorade (for reference) | 12 fl oz | ~160 mg | ~50 mg | ~21 g | Sports drink, high sugar |

A few things jump out:

- **Pedialyte, DripDrop, Electrolit, and Dioralyte are all built around the same idea**: enough sodium to matter, a little glucose to pull it in, and not so much sugar that it slows absorption.
- **Liquid IV sits close to that group** but with more sugar per serving, which is part of why it tastes better.
- **LMNT is in a different category.** It has a lot of sodium and no sugar. That's useful for heavy sweaters and low-carb eaters, less ideal for someone with a sensitive stomach.
- **Nuun is light.** It's a flavored water with modest electrolytes, good for topping up, not for real dehydration.
- **Gatorade is mostly sugar water** with a little sodium. It isn't useless, but it's the weakest rehydrator on the list.

## Pedialyte for a Hangover

Pedialyte was designed for children with vomiting and diarrhea, which is why it works well for adults who are genuinely dehydrated. Its sodium-to-sugar balance follows medical oral rehydration guidelines, and it comes in ready-to-drink bottles, powder packs, and freezer pops (which are surprisingly handy if you're nauseous).

**Pros:**

- Formula is closest to medical ORS of any widely sold brand
- Easy to find in pharmacies and grocery stores
- Lower sugar than sports drinks
- Store-brand versions with the same formula cost much less

**Cons:**

- Many people find the taste salty or flat
- Ready-to-drink bottles are bulky and pricier per serving than powder
- Some "advanced" versions add sweeteners or different ingredients, so the formula varies by product line

If you're deciding between Pedialyte and a sports drink specifically, we compare the two in depth in our [Pedialyte vs Gatorade guide](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover).

## Liquid IV for a Hangover

Liquid IV is the brand most people think of first, mostly because of its marketing. The "Hydration Multiplier" is an ORS-style powder: sodium, potassium, glucose, and some vitamins (vitamin C and B vitamins, depending on the flavor). The company calls its sodium-glucose ratio "Cellular Transport Technology," but that's a brand name for the same sodium-glucose absorption mechanism that every oral rehydration solution relies on. It isn't a separate scientific discovery.

**Pros:**

- Tastes better than most ORS products, so you'll actually drink it
- Sticks are compact and travel well
- Electrolyte content is meaningful, not a token amount

**Cons:**

- More sugar per serving than Pedialyte or DripDrop
- More expensive per serving than store-brand ORS
- The added vitamins don't have good evidence behind them for hangovers

Liquid IV also sells a "Sugar-Free" version and a "Sleep" version. The sugar-free one swaps glucose for sugar alcohols and other sweeteners, which removes the glucose that helps sodium absorption. That makes it a less efficient rehydrator, though still better than nothing. Avoid combining the Sleep version with alcohol the same night, since it contains sleep-promoting ingredients and alcohol is already a sedative.

## DripDrop for a Hangover

DripDrop was developed by a doctor for treating dehydration, and it markets itself as a medical-grade oral rehydration solution. Its formula is similar to Pedialyte: moderate sodium, some potassium, and a small amount of sugar. It comes as powder sticks you mix into a smaller amount of water (often 8 ounces), which makes the solution more concentrated per sip.

**Pros:**

- ORS-style formula that follows the same absorption principle as Pedialyte
- Many people find it tastes better than Pedialyte
- Small serving size is easier to get down when you're queasy

**Cons:**

- Usually pricier per serving than Pedialyte powder
- Small serving means you'll need several to replace a real fluid deficit
- Less widely stocked in stores than Pedialyte

DripDrop is a good choice if your hangover comes with nausea. Small, frequent sips of a proper ORS are the standard approach for keeping fluids down when your stomach is upset. Our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers that in more detail.

## LMNT for a Hangover

LMNT is a sugar-free electrolyte mix with a big dose of sodium (around 1,000 mg per stick), a modest amount of potassium, and some magnesium. It was designed for people on low-carb diets and athletes who sweat a lot, and it has a loyal following in both groups.

**Pros:**

- No sugar, which suits keto and low-carb eaters
- High sodium is genuinely useful if you've lost a lot through sweat
- Clean ingredient list
- Can be diluted in more water to taste

**Cons:**

- No glucose, so it doesn't use the sodium-glucose absorption boost that ORS relies on
- Very salty at full strength, which can be hard on an unsettled stomach
- 1,000 mg of sodium is a lot for one drink, and not a good idea if you have high blood pressure, heart failure, or kidney disease, or have been told to limit salt
- Expensive per serving

For a hangover, LMNT works best diluted in a larger glass of water and paired with something to eat (toast or crackers give you the carbohydrate it lacks). If salty drinks make you gag when you're hungover, pick something else.

## Electrolit for a Hangover

Electrolit is a ready-to-drink oral rehydration solution made in Mexico, now sold widely in US grocery and convenience stores. It's formulated as a medical-style ORS, with sodium, potassium, and glucose, and it comes in a large bottle in a long list of flavors. It has become popular as a hangover drink partly because it's sold right by the checkout in many stores.

**Pros:**

- ORS-style formula, closer to Pedialyte than to Gatorade
- Many people find it tastes better than Pedialyte
- Large ready-to-drink bottle, nothing to mix

**Cons:**

- Bulky and heavy to carry or stockpile
- Flavors and formulas vary, so check the label
- Usually costs more per serving than powder options

If you like the idea of Pedialyte but can't stand the taste, Electrolit is the most direct swap.

## Electrolyte Tablets and Nuun for a Hangover

Electrolyte tablets, with Nuun as the best-known brand, drop into a glass of water and fizz. A Nuun Sport tablet has around 300 mg of sodium, a bit of potassium and magnesium, and very little sugar.

**Pros:**

- Cheapest and most portable option, easy to keep in a bag or travel kit
- Low sugar and low calorie
- Pleasant, lightly fizzy taste

**Cons:**

- Lighter electrolyte dose than ORS products
- Almost no glucose, so absorption is less efficient than with a true ORS
- The fizz can bother an upset stomach

Tablets are fine for a mild hangover where you mostly just need to drink more water and want it to taste of something. If you've been vomiting or feel properly dried out, a real ORS is the better tool. There are also dedicated ORS tablets and salt tablets aimed at athletes. Salt tablets alone (without water and some carbohydrate) aren't a good hangover choice, because they can upset your stomach and they don't hydrate you by themselves.

## Dioralyte for a Hangover (UK and Europe)

Dioralyte is the pharmacy oral rehydration sachet most people in the UK know. Each sachet is mixed into 200 ml of water and provides sodium, potassium, chloride, citrate, and a small amount of glucose, in line with medical rehydration guidance. Similar products are sold under other names in Europe and Australia, and many pharmacies sell their own versions.

**Pros:**

- A real medical ORS, available from any pharmacy
- Inexpensive, especially own-brand versions
- Small sachets travel easily

**Cons:**

- Taste is functional at best
- Small serving per sachet

For a reader in the UK, Dioralyte is the straightforward answer to "what's the Pedialyte equivalent?" It does the same job.

## Which Electrolyte Drink Is Actually Best for a Hangover?

There isn't one winner for everyone. Here's how to choose based on how you feel:

| Your morning | Best pick | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Mild headache, dry mouth, a bit tired | Water plus a Nuun tablet, or Liquid IV | You mostly need fluid. Pick whatever you'll drink. |
| Properly dried out: dark urine, dizzy when standing | Pedialyte, DripDrop, Electrolit, or Dioralyte | Proper ORS replaces fluid and sodium most efficiently. |
| Nauseous or have vomited | DripDrop or Pedialyte, in small sips | Small, frequent sips of ORS are the standard way to keep fluids down. |
| Low-carb diet or sweated heavily (dancing, heat, a festival) | LMNT diluted in extra water, with some food | Lots of sodium, no sugar. |
| Watching sugar but don't want LMNT's salt | Nuun or a sugar-free mix | Lighter on both sodium and sugar. |
| On a budget | Store-brand ORS powder | Same formula as the big brands for less. |

The single most useful rule: **a drink you'll actually finish beats a perfect formula you won't.** If Pedialyte makes you gag, a tastier option you can drink steadily will help you more.

### What about a homemade version?

You can make a basic oral rehydration drink at home with water, a little salt, and a little sugar. The ratios matter, though. Too much salt or sugar can make dehydration worse rather than better, so follow a tested recipe (the WHO and UNICEF publish one) rather than guessing. For most people after a night out, a store-bought ORS is easier and more reliable.

## How to Use an Electrolyte Drink After Drinking

A few habits make these drinks work better:

- **Sip, don't chug.** Large amounts at once can trigger nausea, especially after vomiting. A few mouthfuls every few minutes works better.
- **Start before bed if you can.** A glass of water or an electrolyte drink before you sleep helps you start the morning less behind. We cover the timing question in detail in our guide on [whether to take electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking).
- **Eat something.** Food provides carbohydrates and electrolytes of its own, and it helps settle your blood sugar.
- **Don't overdo the sodium.** Two or three servings across a morning is plenty for most people. More isn't better, and very high sodium intake is a real concern if you have blood pressure, heart, or kidney problems.
- **Watch your urine.** Pale yellow means you're doing fine. Still dark after several hours of drinking fluids, or barely urinating at all, is a reason to get checked.

## What Electrolyte Drinks Can't Do

To be clear about the limits:

- **They don't speed up how fast your body clears alcohol.** Your liver sets that pace. No drink changes it in a meaningful way.
- **They don't sober you up.** If you're still drunk, you're still drunk, even if you feel a bit more alert.
- **They don't fix the inflammation, poor sleep, or acetaldehyde effects** that drive most of a hangover.
- **There is no good evidence that drinking electrolytes alongside alcohol prevents a hangover** on its own. Staying hydrated through the night helps you avoid the dehydration piece, but it doesn't stop the rest.

If you find yourself relying on electrolyte drinks most weekends, the bigger gains usually come from upstream habits: eating before you drink, alternating alcoholic drinks with water, choosing lighter drinks, and stopping earlier. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through the ones with the best evidence, and our roundup of the [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) covers options beyond electrolytes. If you prefer something natural, [coconut water](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) is high in potassium but low in sodium, so it's a weaker rehydrator than ORS on its own.

## Where DHM Fits In

Electrolyte drinks address the fluid you lost. They don't touch how your body handles the alcohol itself. That's where some people add **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, including the acetaldehyde step. The honest status of the evidence: encouraging animal and lab research, limited human data. It's promising, not proven, and it's no reason to drink more.

If you want to try it, the two picks we rate highest are [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which pairs DHM with electrolytes, so it covers some of the hydration angle as well, and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. A sensible routine is DHM with your drinks, water between them, and an electrolyte drink before bed or the next morning if you're dried out.

## The Bottom Line

- For real dehydration after drinking, a medical-style oral rehydration solution (Pedialyte, DripDrop, Electrolit, Dioralyte) is the most efficient choice.
- Liquid IV is a close, tastier alternative with more sugar. LMNT is very high in sodium with no sugar and suits a narrower group. Nuun tablets are fine for mild mornings.
- Gatorade works, but it's the weakest rehydrator of the common options because of its high sugar and low sodium.
- Electrolytes help with the dehydration part of a hangover only. They don't clear alcohol faster or fix inflammation and poor sleep.
- Can't keep fluids down, barely urinating, confused, faint, or getting worse instead of better? Get medical care. If someone is hard to wake or breathing oddly after heavy drinking, call 911.

**Related reading:** [homemade electrolyte drink](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink), [LMNT vs Liquid I.V.](/never-hungover/lmnt-vs-liquid-iv), [Electrolit vs Pedialyte](/never-hungover/electrolit-vs-pedialyte).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best electrolyte drink for a hangover?**

For real dehydration, a medical-style oral rehydration solution such as Pedialyte, DripDrop, Electrolit, or Dioralyte is the most efficient choice, because its sodium and glucose balance helps your gut absorb water. Liquid IV is a close alternative with more sugar and a better taste. For a mild hangover, any of these, or water with an electrolyte tablet, is fine. Pick the one you'll actually drink.

**Is Liquid IV or Pedialyte better for a hangover?**

They're closer than the marketing suggests. Both use the same sodium-glucose absorption principle. Pedialyte has less sugar and a formula closer to medical guidelines, so it's slightly better if you're properly dehydrated or have been vomiting. Liquid IV has a bit more sodium and sugar per serving and tastes better, which matters if you'd otherwise not finish your drink. Either is a reasonable choice for a typical hangover.

**Is LMNT good for a hangover?**

It can help, especially if you sweated a lot or eat low-carb, because it's high in sodium with no sugar. The downsides are that it lacks the glucose that speeds absorption and it's very salty at full strength, which can be hard on an upset stomach. Try it diluted in extra water with some food. Avoid it if you have high blood pressure, heart failure, or kidney disease, or have been told to limit salt.

**Do electrolyte tablets like Nuun work for a hangover?**

They help with mild hangovers where you mainly need to drink more water. Nuun tablets have a modest amount of sodium and almost no sugar, so they're lighter than a true oral rehydration solution. If you've been vomiting or feel properly dried out, Pedialyte, DripDrop, or a similar ORS is a better fit.

**What is the UK equivalent of Pedialyte for a hangover?**

Dioralyte, which is sold in pharmacies across the UK, is a medical oral rehydration sachet that does the same job as Pedialyte. Pharmacy own-brand rehydration sachets work the same way and usually cost less.

**Can electrolyte drinks prevent a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that electrolyte drinks prevent a hangover on their own. Staying hydrated can reduce the dehydration piece, such as dry mouth and some headaches, but most hangover symptoms come from inflammation, poor sleep, and the effects of alcohol's breakdown products, which electrolytes don't address.

**Is Gatorade good enough for a hangover?**

It's better than nothing, and if it's all you have, drink it. But regular Gatorade has much more sugar and much less sodium than an oral rehydration solution, so it's a weaker rehydrator. If you're properly dehydrated, an ORS like Pedialyte is the better choice.

**When should I see a doctor instead of drinking electrolytes?**

Get medical help if you can't keep fluids down for several hours, you're vomiting repeatedly or see blood, you've barely urinated in 8 hours or more, you feel faint or confused, or you're getting worse rather than better as the day goes on. If someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin after heavy drinking, call 911. That may be alcohol poisoning.
